name: Lajkonik
description: The Lajkonik is a hobby-horse rider of Kraków, a masked figure dressed as a Tatar warrior who parades the Old Town on the octave of Corpus Christi, striking onlookers with a wooden mace for luck. The procession commemorates the defeat of a Mongol raid, and the figure has been a beloved Kraków festival emblem for centuries.
source: Ethnographic studies of Kraków folk festivals

name: Rogatywka
description: The rogatywka is a four-pointed peaked cap of Polish tradition, evolved from the konfederatka worn by Bar Confederation troops in 1768 and later the standard Polish military cap. Its four corners mark the four sides of the world, and it remains a national and military symbol worn in parades and folk ensembles.
source: Histories of Polish military dress

name: Wycinanka
description: Wycinanka is Polish folk paper-cutting, most famously the colourful layered cutouts of Łowicz, made with sheep shears from dyed paper. Designs show birds, suns, flowers and village scenes, and were pasted on walls and beams to brighten rural homes, particularly in Mazovia and Kurpie regions.
source: Studies of Polish folk paper-cutting

name: Kraków Szopka
description: The Kraków szopka is a colourful Nativity crib built as a miniature of Kraków's architecture, with towers, spires and gilt foil, crafted by krakowianie and judged each December in a contest at the Rynek. The tradition, inscribed by UNESCO in 2018, blends the Nativity scene with civic pride and Christmas carolling.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Kraków ethnography

name: Pomlázka
description: The pomlázka is a braided whip of willow twigs used on Easter Monday in the Czech lands, when boys lightly switch girls to keep them fresh and healthy, receiving painted eggs in return. Made of eight to twelve woven twigs bound with ribbon, it carries an old spring-renewal meaning in Czech folk custom.
source: Czech and Slovak ethnography of Easter customs

name: Czech Glass Christmas Ornaments
description: Czech glass Christmas ornaments are hand-blown and hand-painted glass baubles produced around Jablonec nad Nisou since the mid-19th century. Tiny beads and figurines are strung for the tree, and the region's skilled glassworkers made Christmas ornaments a famous export prized for their delicate silvering and colours.
source: Histories of Bohemian glassmaking

name: Fujara
description: The fujara is a long overtone flute of Slovak shepherds, up to two metres long, made from elder or maple wood with a unique air duct. Played while standing, it produces a deep humming bass; its sound and technique were inscribed by UNESCO in 2008 as a living shepherd tradition.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnomusicology

name: Drotárstvo (Wire Craft)
description: Drotárstvo, or wire craft, is the Slovak art of reinforcing cracked pottery and glass with fine iron wire, practised by travelling drotár craftsmen from the 18th century. Wire-bound jugs, bottles and bowls became folk masterpieces, and the craft was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2019.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Slovak ethnography

name: Valaška
description: The valaška is the small shepherd's axe of the Carpathian Highlands, a light axe on a long decorated wooden handle used as a staff, tool and weapon by Slovak bača shepherds. Legend credits it as the weapon of Jánošík, and it became a badge of the highland shepherd's life.
material: forged iron blade, carved wood handle
source: Slovak folklore and highland ethnography

name: Bogrács
description: A bogrács is a black cast-iron cauldron hung over an open fire, the essential vessel of Hungarian gulyás and pörkölt cooking. Its three legs and swing-arm let cooks stir the stew over flame, and bogrács gatherings are a central social ritual of Hungarian outdoor cookery.
source: Hungarian culinary and folk ethnography

name: Matyó Embroidery
description: Matyó embroidery is the vivid floral needlework of Mezőkövesd in Hungary, with large rose, tulip and peony motifs in red, blue and green silk on white linen. Worn on festive costumes and home textiles, the technique was inscribed by UNESCO in 2012 as a living community craft.
source: UNESCO intangible heritage files and Hungarian textile studies

name: Székely Kapu
description: The Székely kapu is the richly carved wooden gate of the Hungarian Székely villages of Transylvania, its great oak posts carved with suns, tulips, the tree of life and heraldic symbols. A marriage gate stands before the house and a small gate for the dead leads to the yard, making each carving a family record.
source: Hungarian and Székely ethnography of folk architecture

name: Cifraszűr
description: The cifraszűr is the embroidered shepherd's coat of the Hungarian Great Plain, a knee-length wool felt cloak covered with appliquéd floral and rosette patterns in coloured wool. Worn by herdsmen and hung as a sign of rank, its rich surface made it a prized gift and heirloom.
material: white wool felt, coloured wool thread
source: Hungarian folk costume studies

name: Crown of Saint Stephen
description: The Holy Crown of Hungary is the golden coronation crown of Saint Stephen I, decorated with cloisonné enamel plaques and a bent cross. Kept in the Hungarian Parliament in Budapest, it symbolises Hungarian statehood and was used to crown kings until 1916, though its age and true origin remain debated.
aliases: Crown of Saint Stephen of Hungary
source: Academic studies of the Hungarian coronation insignia

name: Martenitsa
description: The martenitsa is a Bulgarian talisman of twisted red and white yarn, with a small pendant, given on 1 March to wish health and spring. Worn on the wrist until a stork or blossom appears, it honours Baba Marta, and the shared custom is inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.
source: Bulgarian ethnography of spring customs and UNESCO files

name: Kukeri
description: The kukeri are Bulgarian winter ritual figures, men dressed in sheepskin costumes with tall carved wooden masks, animal hides and heavy bronze bells who dance through villages at New Year and before Lent to drive away evil spirits and bring fertility. The rite is strongest in the Pernik and Shoppe regions.
material: sheepskin, carved wood, goat hair, bronze bells
source: Bulgarian ethnography of winter ritual customs

name: Gaida
description: The gaida is the Bulgarian bagpipe, a goatskin bag with a chanter and drone, played at weddings, festivals and shepherds' pastures. Its bright, reedy voice leads horo dances, and it is considered the most beloved national instrument of Bulgarian folk music.
source: Bulgarian ethnomusicology

name: Mărțișor
description: Mărțișorul is the Romanian March talisman, a red-and-white silk thread tied with a small charm or coin, offered on 1 March for health and good luck. Worn through the month and then hung on a fruit tree, it welcomes spring, and is shared in the UNESCO-inscribed 1 March customs.
material: red and white silk thread, metal charm or coin
source: Romanian ethnography of spring customs and UNESCO files

name: Troiță
description: Troița is the Romanian wayside cross, a hand-carved oak cross sheltered by a small roof, placed at roadsides, springs and crossroads to guard travellers and honour the dead. Maramureș carvers cover them with vines and geometric rosettes, making each troiță a prayer in wood.
source: Romanian ethnography of folk architecture and religion

name: Dacian Gold Bracelets
description: The Dacian gold bracelets are spiral gold arm rings from the kingdom of Dacia, cast in the mid-1st century BC and buried at Sarmizegetusa Regia. Looted in 2000 and partly recovered, they now belong to the Historical Treasury of the National History Museum in Bucharest and are masterpieces of Dacian goldwork.
source: Archaeological studies of the Sarmizegetusa Regia treasure

name: Šajkača
description: The šajkača is the Serbian cap with a raised V-shaped crown, descended from the cloth caps of the 18th-century šajkaši river troops who patrolled the Danube. Worn by Serbian soldiers and peasants, and in the Serbian military tradition, it became a national headgear symbol.
source: Histories of Serbian military dress and ethnography

name: Pirot Kilim
description: The Pirot kilim is a handwoven wool rug of the town of Pirot in southern Serbia, made on a vertical loom with geometric medallions and borders in red, black, green and white. Woven for centuries for floors, walls and weddings, it is counted a national symbol of Serbian weaving.
source: Serbian textile and craft studies

name: Opanak
description: The opanak is traditional Serbian peasant footwear, a soft leather moccasin with a turned-up pointed toe and leather straps, hand-made and waterproof. Its curling toe, worn for walking in grass and hills, made it a marker of Serbian village identity and folk dress.
source: Serbian folk dress studies

name: Ohrid Pearl
description: Ohrid pearls are handmade jewellery pearls of North Macedonia, formed by layering fish-scale essence over a mother-of-pearl core, made in Ohrid workshops for about a century. Their warm lustre and entirely manual method made them a signature craft of Ohrid and the region's jewellers.
source: Macedonian craft and jewellery studies

name: Dvojanka
description: The dvojanka is a North Macedonian double flute, two parallel pipes carved from one piece of wood or bone with fingerholes on one pipe, played by shepherds. Its paired pipes sound a drone with the melody, and it accompanies Macedonian pastoral and festive music.
source: Macedonian ethnomusicology

name: Chokha (Georgian Men's Coat)
description: Woolen coat of Georgian men with a fitted waist, flared skirt and rows of decorative cartridge loops (gazyr) across the chest. Worn since at least the 17th century across the Caucasus, the chokha remains the emblem of Georgian national dress and is now reserved mostly for festivals, dance and ceremony.
source: Georgian National Museum, Tbilisi; ethnographic dress studies of the Caucasus

name: Kantsi (Georgian Drinking Horn)
description: Drinking vessel of the Georgian highlands carved from the curved horn of an ox or mountain goat, sometimes mounted in chased silver, and used for wine at feasts. Raised during the traditional Georgian toast, the kantsi is especially associated with Svaneti and Khevsureti feast custom; the largest examples rest on a stand or are passed from hand to hand around the table of drinking companions.
material: ox or goat horn, chased silver (festive examples)
source: Russian Museum of Ethnography collections; Georgian feast (supra) custom studies

name: Panduri (Georgian Three-String Lute)
description: Three-stringed fretted lute of Georgia with a shallow wooden body and gut or nylon strings, played to accompany songs and instrumental pieces. Traditionally hung on the wall of the house when not in use, the panduri accompanies both men's and women's singing; with the larger four-string chonguri it is the most common plucked instrument of Georgian folk music and an emblem of Georgian tradition.
material: mulberry or other wood, gut/nylon strings
source: Georgian folk music tradition; hangebi.ge folk instrument documentation

name: Chonguri (Georgian Four-String Lute)
description: Four-stringed fretless lute of western Georgia carved from a single block of walnut or maple, with a shallow bowl body and a shorter drone string called zili. Associated with the Megrel and Gurian lowlands, the chonguri traditionally accompanied women's songs and the evening work gatherings (nadi); its strings are named after the voices of Georgian polyphonic song.
material: walnut or maple, spruce soundboard, nylon strings
source: Smithsonian 'Georgian Chonguri' object of the day; Georgian folk instrument studies (Arakishvili)

name: Chuniri (Svan Bowed Fiddle)
description: Three-string bowed fiddle of the Georgian mountain province of Svaneti, with a circular or tubular body and a skin soundboard, played to accompany songs and dances. Because bowed strings sustain long notes, the chuniri (and its two-string cousin the chianuri) can stand in for a singing voice in Svan hunting songs and choral music; it is one of the two traditional bowed instruments of Georgia.
material: wood body, skin soundboard, horsehair strings
source: Wikipedia 'Chuniri'; Georgian folk music instrument documentation

name: Qvevri (Georgian Wine Vessel)
description: Large egg-shaped earthenware vessel used to make and age Georgian wine, buried up to the neck in the cellar floor with only the rim above ground. Grapes, must and skins ferment and rest in the qvevri for months, giving the wine its tannic, amber character; the method is at least 8,000 years old, and UNESCO inscribed ancient Georgian qvevri wine-making in 2013.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Ancient Georgian traditional Qvevri wine-making method' (2013)

name: Khachkar (Armenian Cross-Stone)
description: Freestanding stele of Armenia carved from a single slab of local stone, usually tuff, with an ornamented cross set over a rosette or wheel of eternity and covered in interlace, vine and pomegranate motifs. Erected from the 9th century as tombstones, memorials and church stones, khachkars link the secular and the divine; in 2010 UNESCO inscribed their art on its intangible heritage list.
material: volcanic tuff or other local stone
source: UNESCO ICH 'Armenian cross-stones art. Symbolism and craftsmanship of Khachkars' (2010)

name: Duduk (Armenian Double-Reed Flute)
description: Double-reed woodwind of Armenia made from apricot wood, with a wide interchangeable reed, played with circular breathing to produce a warm, vocal tone. The duduk accompanies song, dance and lament and is central to Armenian instrumental tradition; its music was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2008.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Duduk and its music' (2008)

name: Tar (Azerbaijani Long-Necked Lute)
description: Long-necked plucked lute of Azerbaijan with a figure-of-eight wooden body, a lambskin soundboard and six steel strings, held diagonally and plucked with a plectrum. The tar leads the mugham trio and accompanies ashiq song; its craftsmanship and performance art were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2012. It is one of the few national instruments for which Azerbaijani composers wrote concert works.
material: mulberry wood, lambskin soundboard, steel strings
source: UNESCO ICH 'Craftsmanship and performance art of the Tar' (2012)

name: Kamancha (Azerbaijani Spike Fiddle)
description: Bowed spike fiddle of Azerbaijan, with a spherical wooden body covered in fish- or lambskin, a long neck and four steel strings, played upright with the bow. Alongside the tar it leads the mugham trio and folk ensembles; the art of crafting and playing the kamancha was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2017. Its small, bright tone carries well in indoor ensembles.
material: walnut or mulberry wood, skin soundboard, steel strings
source: UNESCO ICH 'Art of crafting and playing with kamancha' (2017)

name: Kelaghayi (Azerbaijani Silk Headscarf)
description: Square silk headscarf of Azerbaijani women, dyed and decorated with woodblock-printed border ornaments, most often the buta (teardrop) motif, with white, red and dark colours marking age and occasion. Woven mainly in Sheki and the Basgal settlement, the kelaghayi is worn at weddings, mourning and daily life; its making and symbolism were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2014.
era: silk tradition from c. 7th century; kelaghayi to present
source: UNESCO ICH 'Traditional art and symbolism of Kelaghayi' (2014)

name: Shebeke (Sheki Stained-Glass Lattice)
description: Stained-glass window of Sheki, Azerbaijan, made by fitting hundreds of small pieces of coloured glass into a lattice of walnut strips that interlock without glue or nails. The finest example survives in the 1762 Sheki Khan's Palace, whose roughly 190 windows hold up to 5,000 fragments of glass; masters call the craft 'the art of patience', as a single panel can take months.
source: UNESCO World Heritage 'Historic Centre of Sheki with the Khan's Palace' (2019); Art of Shebeke (national ICH inventory)

name: Shahmaran Amulet
description: Amulet bearing the image of Shahmaran, the serpent queen of Caucasian and Anatolian legend, a figure with a woman's head and a serpent body, worn or hung for protection against the evil eye. Amulets, jewellery and wall paintings of the serpent queen are attested across centuries, and her image survives in major collections such as the British Museum and in Azerbaijani amulets and carpet motifs.
material: silver or brass, engraved or painted serpent-queen image
source: British Museum collection (E AF.77); Shahmaran legend of Azerbaijan and Anatolia

name: Lahij Copperware
description: Copper and brass vessels of the Lahij craft town of Azerbaijan, including ewers, basins, cauldrons and trays hammered from a single sheet of metal and engraved with geometric and floral patterns, often coated with a silvery tin alloy. Copper craftsmanship of Lahij was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2015; the trade flourished in the 19th century, when Lahij copperware was sold along the Silk Road.
source: UNESCO ICH 'Copper craftsmanship of Lahij' (2015)

name: Azerbaijani Carpet
description: Handwoven knotted carpet of Azerbaijan, whose regional schools include Caucasian, Tabriz, Karabakh, Shirvan and Baku weaving, with distinctive motifs such as the buta, dragon and stylised garden. Carpet weaving is a women's craft passed down in families; the traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2010, and carpets remain the country's best-known craft.
material: wool pile, cotton warp, natural dyes
era: attested from the Middle Ages; classical schools 16th-19th century
source: UNESCO ICH 'Traditional art of Azerbaijani carpet weaving' (2010)
